title: Hermas
lead: Hermas is the name of a Christian in Rome whom Paul greets (Romans 16:14), and of the Roman Christian who wrote the Shepherd of Hermas in the second century and says that the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda. Whether they are the same man was argued in the early church.

sections.b: At the end of Romans Paul greets Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers with them (Romans 16:14). Nothing more is said of him in the New Testament. Origen thought he was the writer of the Shepherd: "I think, however, that this Hermas is the writer of that little book called the Shepherd" (Commentary on Romans 10.31, in the Latin of Rufinus's abridged translation, as Westcott quotes it). Eusebius (Church History 3.3.6) and Jerome (Lives of Illustrious Men 10) report it as what others say. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates the Apostle Hermas of the Seventy on May 31, as a bishop of Philippopolis in Thrace, and says that "according to Tradition" he wrote the Shepherd. Westcott (1896) called the identification "nothing more than a conjecture" of Origen's.

sections.h: Hermas the writer of the Shepherd
sections.b: The writer tells his own story. The man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda in Rome (Shepherd of Hermas 1:1); Lake calls the sentence "hardly intelligible" as it stands and takes it to mean, "presumably," that Hermas "was born a slave." He had a business, a wife and children, and his children had sinned badly, even betraying their parents (Shepherd of Hermas 6:2–3). Visions came to him on the road out of Rome: Rhoda from heaven, the Church as an old woman, the tower, the beast, and the Shepherd, the angel of repentance, who came to live with him (Shepherd of Hermas 25:1–2). The Muratorian Fragment says Hermas wrote "very recently, in our own times," while his brother Pius was bishop of Rome, about 148 in Lake's dating; Chapman (1910) adds the Liberian list of Roman bishops and a Latin poem against Marcion as further witnesses, and thinks all three "are probably citing the same papal catalogue." The Fragment's own date is disputed (see the Shepherd of Hermas page). Chapman notes that the name, a short form of names such as Hermogenes, suited a slave, and that "we cannot even be sure that the writer's name was really Hermas."

sections.b: Hermas's message was that Christians who had sinned after baptism could still repent and be received, once (Shepherd of Hermas 6:4–5; Shepherd of Hermas 31:6). Lake calls this "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance"; Tertullian, as a Montanist, attacked the book as "the only one that loves adulterers." Both views are set out on the book's opening page.
